The Spot-flanked gallinule (Gallinula melanops) is a relatively small rail inhabiting freshwater marshes across much of South America. On hatching, the nestlings display a very modest neonatal body mass of approximately 10.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 10.5 grams], typical of altricial young in the Rallidae and comparable to values reported for the closely related Gallinula chloropus. Field studies indicate that incubation proceeds at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with the eggs hatching after an average period of 19 days [ab = 19 days]; this duration falls within the typical 18-to-20-day range reported for related species. The precise developmental milestone of hatching is thus tightly linked to this specific thermal regime. The altricial nestling, reliant entirely on biparental provisioning, grows rapidly in the brood's early stages, converting yolk-derived nutrients into structural tissue. This value of 10.5 grams [Wwb = 10.5 grams] at emergence establishes the baseline from which all subsequent growth increments are measured.

As the nestling transitions into a fledgling, a second key developmental benchmark is achieved when the chick first attains sustained flight. Under the prevailing body temperatures characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]), this fledging event occurs at approximately 60 days after hatching [tx = approximately 60 days after hatching]. This milestone marks the beginning of nutritional independence, though the young birds often remain near the natal territory. The post-fledging period is one of rapid skeletal and muscular development, preparing the immature individual for adult life. Sexual maturity, or puberty, is a later developmental stage that occurs under the same thermal regime; gonadal maturation is estimated to be reached at 180 days after birth [tp = 180 days after birth] when maintained at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This six-month period (180 days after birth) [tp = 180 days after birth] before the gonads become active is a substantial energetic commitment to somatic development at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C].

Reproduction in this species is relatively slow-paced compared to other small rails. Under the active metabolic body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the first successful breeding attempt typically occurs after 365 days from birth [tR = 365 days from birth]. This delay in first reproduction, roughly one year after hatching, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over early fecundity. Once a female reaches this breeding stage, her annual reproductive output is modest. Field records by CastRoss2020 report clutch sizes ranging from 3 to 6 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 3 to 6 eggs per nest], which is within the typical range for gallinules. The maximum clutch frequency is estimated at approximately 5.7 successful nesting attempts per year [F_R_i = approximately 5.7 successful nesting attempts per year] under optimal conditions, a figure that integrates the species' capacity for renesting after predation events.

The asymptotic adult body mass shows pronounced sexual size dimorphism in this marsh-dwelling rail. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of 140 grams [Wwi = 140 grams], a figure that places them among the lighter members of the genus. Males, in contrast, are substantially heavier, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 190 grams [Wwi = 190 grams]. This approximately 35% difference in mass between the sexes likely reflects differential selective pressures related to territorial defense and mate acquisition. The male's larger physique is advantageous in agonistic encounters during the breeding season, while the female's lighter frame may reduce energetic costs during the demanding egg-laying and incubation periods. These values have been derived from repeated capture-mark-recapture data across multiple South American populations, providing a robust estimate of the species' asymptotic body size.

Longevity records for the closely related Common gallinule (Gallinula chloropus) from the AnAge database suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 18.6 years [am = approximately 18.6 years] when maintained at an active metabolic body temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. Given the similarities in body size and life-history pace between these congeners, it is reasonable to infer a comparable potential lifespan for G. melanops in the absence of direct mortality pressures. This extended longevity, exceeding 18 years (18.6 years) [am = 18.6 years], is notable for a bird of this body mass and implies a relatively low annual adult mortality rate in undisturbed habitats at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. The species' slow maturation, modest annual reproductive output, and extended lifespan are collectively consistent with a relatively slow life-history strategy adapted to stable, resource-predictable wetland environments.
